claim: A wide variety of human diseases are associated with loss of microbial diversity in the human gut.
source: A wide variety of human diseases are associated with loss of microbial diversity in the human gut, inspiring a great interest in the diagnostic or therapeutic potential of the microbiota.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific consensus about disease-microbiome associations.

claim: The ecological forces that drive diversity reduction in disease states remain unclear.
source: However, the ecological forces that drive diversity reduction in disease states remain unclear, rendering it difficult to ascertain the role of the microbiota in disease emergence or severity.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current understanding based on the state of the field.

claim: High metabolic independence (HMI) is a distinguishing characteristic of microbial communities associated with individuals diagnosed with IBD.
source: We found that high metabolic independence (HMI) is a distinguishing characteristic of microbial communities associated with individuals diagnosed with IBD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the analysis of over 400 gut metagenomes.

claim: A classifier trained using normalized copy numbers of 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules distinguished states of health vs IBD.
source: A classifier we trained using the normalized copy numbers of 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules not only distinguished states of health vs IBD, but also tracked the recovery of the gut microbiome following antibiotic treatment, suggesting that HMI is a hallmark of microbial communities in stressed gut environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the classifier performance data presented in the study.

claim: The classifier trained on HMI-associated metabolic modules tracked the recovery of the gut microbiome following antibiotic treatment.
source: A classifier we trained using the normalized copy numbers of 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules not only distinguished states of health vs IBD, but also tracked the recovery of the gut microbiome following antibiotic treatment, suggesting that HMI is a hallmark of microbial communities in stressed gut environments.
evidence: This is supported by application of the classifier to the Palleja et al., 2018 antibiotic treatment dataset.

claim: HMI is a hallmark of microbial communities in stressed gut environments.
source: A classifier we trained using the normalized copy numbers of 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules not only distinguished states of health vs IBD, but also tracked the recovery of the gut microbiome following antibiotic treatment, suggesting that HMI is a hallmark of microbial communities in stressed gut environments.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the classifier's performance across different stress conditions (IBD and antibiotics).

claim: The gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth.
source: This gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth and plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Maynard et al., 2012), extracting dietary nutrients (Hijova, 2019), providing protection against pathogens (Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013), metabolizing drugs (Zimmermann et al., 2019), and more (Knight et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The gut microbiome plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning.
source: This gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth and plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Maynard et al., 2012), extracting dietary nutrients (Hijova, 2019), providing protection against pathogens (Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013), metabolizing drugs (Zimmermann et al., 2019), and more (Knight et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belkaid and Hand, 2014 and Maynard et al., 2012.

claim: The gut microbiome extracts dietary nutrients.
source: This gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth and plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Maynard et al., 2012), extracting dietary nutrients (Hijova, 2019), providing protection against pathogens (Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013), metabolizing drugs (Zimmermann et al., 2019), and more (Knight et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hijova, 2019.

claim: The gut microbiome provides protection against pathogens.
source: This gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth and plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Maynard et al., 2012), extracting dietary nutrients (Hijova, 2019), providing protection against pathogens (Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013), metabolizing drugs (Zimmermann et al., 2019), and more (Knight et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013.

claim: The gut microbiome metabolizes drugs.
source: This gut microbial ecosystem is established almost immediately after birth and plays a lifelong role in human well-being by contributing to immune system maturation and functioning (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Maynard et al., 2012), extracting dietary nutrients (Hijova, 2019), providing protection against pathogens (Khosravi and Mazmanian, 2013), metabolizing drugs (Zimmermann et al., 2019), and more (Knight et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmermann et al., 2019.

claim: There is no universal definition of a healthy gut microbiome.
source: There is no universal definition of a healthy gut microbiome (Fan and Pedersen, 2021), but associations between host disease states and changes in microbial community composition have sparked great interest in the therapeutic potential of gut microbes (Cani, 2018; Sorbara and Pamer, 2022) and led to the emergence of hypotheses that directly link disruptions of the gut microbiome to noncommunicable diseases of complex etiology (Byndloss and Bäumler, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fan and Pedersen, 2021.

claim: Associations between host disease states and changes in microbial community composition have sparked great interest in the therapeutic potential of gut microbes.
source: There is no universal definition of a healthy gut microbiome (Fan and Pedersen, 2021), but associations between host disease states and changes in microbial community composition have sparked great interest in the therapeutic potential of gut microbes (Cani, 2018; Sorbara and Pamer, 2022) and led to the emergence of hypotheses that directly link disruptions of the gut microbiome to noncommunicable diseases of complex etiology (Byndloss and Bäumler, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cani, 2018 and Sorbara and Pamer, 2022.

claim: Hypotheses have emerged that directly link disruptions of the gut microbiome to noncommunicable diseases of complex etiology.
source: There is no universal definition of a healthy gut microbiome (Fan and Pedersen, 2021), but associations between host disease states and changes in microbial community composition have sparked great interest in the therapeutic potential of gut microbes (Cani, 2018; Sorbara and Pamer, 2022) and led to the emergence of hypotheses that directly link disruptions of the gut microbiome to noncommunicable diseases of complex etiology (Byndloss and Bäumler, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Byndloss and Bäumler, 2018.

claim: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) describe a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory disorders.
source: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), which describe a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory disorders (Shan et al., 2022), represent an increasingly common health risk around the globe (Kaplan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shan et al., 2022.

claim: IBDs represent an increasingly common health risk around the globe.
source: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), which describe a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory disorders (Shan et al., 2022), represent an increasingly common health risk around the globe (Kaplan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaplan, 2015.

claim: Studies focusing on individual microbial taxa that typically change in relative abundance in IBD patients have proposed a range of host-microbe interactions that may contribute to disease manifestation and progression.
source: Studies focusing on individual microbial taxa that typically change in relative abundance in IBD patients have proposed a range of host-microbe interactions that may contribute to disease manifestation and progression (Joossens et al., 2011; Schirmer et al., 2019; Henke et al., 2019; Machiels et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joossens et al., 2011; Schirmer et al., 2019; Henke et al., 2019; Machiels et al., 2014.

claim: Within well-constrained cohorts, a large proportion of variability in the taxonomic composition of the microbiota is unexplained.
source: However, even within well-constrained cohorts, a large proportion of variability in the taxonomic composition of the microbiota is unexplained, and the proportion of variability explained by disease status is low (Gevers et al., 2014; Schirmer et al., 2018; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gevers et al., 2014; Schirmer et al., 2018; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019.

claim: The proportion of variability in microbiota taxonomic composition explained by disease status is low.
source: However, even within well-constrained cohorts, a large proportion of variability in the taxonomic composition of the microbiota is unexplained, and the proportion of variability explained by disease status is low (Gevers et al., 2014; Schirmer et al., 2018; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gevers et al., 2014; Schirmer et al., 2018; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019.

claim: Neither individual taxa nor broad changes in microbial community composition yield effective predictors of disease.
source: As neither individual taxa nor broad changes in microbial community composition yield effective predictors of disease (Knox et al., 2019; Lee and Chang, 2021), the role of gut microbes in the etiology of IBD – or the extent to which they are bystanders to disease – remains unclear (Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knox et al., 2019 and Lee and Chang, 2021.

claim: The role of gut microbes in the etiology of IBD remains unclear.
source: As neither individual taxa nor broad changes in microbial community composition yield effective predictors of disease (Knox et al., 2019; Lee and Chang, 2021), the role of gut microbes in the etiology of IBD – or the extent to which they are bystanders to disease – remains unclear (Khan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khan et al., 2019.

claim: The marked decrease in microbial diversity in IBD is often associated with the loss of Firmicutes populations.
source: The marked decrease in microbial diversity in IBD is often associated with the loss of Firmicutes populations and an increased representation of a relatively small number of taxa, such as Bacteroides, Enterococcaceae, and others (Prindiville et al., 2000; Saitoh et al., 2002; Sartor, 2006; Rhodes, 2007; Devkota et al., 2012; Machiels et al., 2014; Vineis et al., 2016; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prindiville et al., 2000; Saitoh et al., 2002; Sartor, 2006; Rhodes, 2007; Devkota et al., 2012; Machiels et al., 2014; Vineis et al., 2016; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019.

claim: The marked decrease in microbial diversity in IBD is associated with an increased representation of a relatively small number of taxa, such as Bacteroides, Enterococcaceae, and others.
source: The marked decrease in microbial diversity in IBD is often associated with the loss of Firmicutes populations and an increased representation of a relatively small number of taxa, such as Bacteroides, Enterococcaceae, and others (Prindiville et al., 2000; Saitoh et al., 2002; Sartor, 2006; Rhodes, 2007; Devkota et al., 2012; Machiels et al., 2014; Vineis et al., 2016; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prindiville et al., 2000; Saitoh et al., 2002; Sartor, 2006; Rhodes, 2007; Devkota et al., 2012; Machiels et al., 2014; Vineis et al., 2016; Lloyd-Price et al., 2019.

claim: A recent metagenome-wide metabolic modeling study revealed a significant loss of cross-feeding partners as a hallmark of IBD.
source: Going beyond taxonomic summaries, a recent metagenome-wide metabolic modeling study revealed a significant loss of cross-feeding partners as a hallmark of IBD, where microbial interactions were disrupted in IBD-associated microbial communities compared to those found in healthy individuals (Marcelino et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marcelino et al., 2023.

claim: Microbial interactions were disrupted in IBD-associated microbial communities compared to those found in healthy individuals.
source: Going beyond taxonomic summaries, a recent metagenome-wide metabolic modeling study revealed a significant loss of cross-feeding partners as a hallmark of IBD, where microbial interactions were disrupted in IBD-associated microbial communities compared to those found in healthy individuals (Marcelino et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marcelino et al., 2023.

claim: The extent of 'metabolic independence' is a determinant of microbial survival in IBD.
source: This observation is in line with another recent work that proposed that the extent of 'metabolic independence' (characterized by the genomic presence of a set of key metabolic modules for the synthesis of essential nutrients) is a determinant of microbial survival in IBD (Watson et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2023.

claim: The study compiled 2893 publicly available stool metagenomes from 13 different studies.
source: We compiled 2893 publicly available stool metagenomes from 13 different studies, 5 of which explicitly studied the IBD gut microbiome (Supplementary file 1a–c).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Five of the 13 studies explicitly studied the IBD gut microbiome.
source: We compiled 2893 publicly available stool metagenomes from 13 different studies, 5 of which explicitly studied the IBD gut microbiome (Supplementary file 1a–c).
evidence: This describes the composition of the dataset.

claim: Samples with less than 25 million reads were excluded to improve the sensitivity and accuracy of downstream analyses.
source: To improve the sensitivity and accuracy of our downstream analyses that depend on metagenomic assembly, we excluded samples with less than 25 million reads, resulting in a set of 408 relatively deeply sequenced metagenomes from 10 studies (26.4 to 61.9 million paired-end reads, with a median value of 37.0, Supplementary file 1b, Appendix 1, Methods), which we de novo assembled individually.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision based on data quality considerations.

claim: The final dataset included 408 relatively deeply sequenced metagenomes from 10 studies.
source: To improve the sensitivity and accuracy of our downstream analyses that depend on metagenomic assembly, we excluded samples with less than 25 million reads, resulting in a set of 408 relatively deeply sequenced metagenomes from 10 studies (26.4 to 61.9 million paired-end reads, with a median value of 37.0, Supplementary file 1b, Appendix 1, Methods), which we de novo assembled individually.
evidence: This describes the final dataset composition.

claim: The final dataset included individuals who were healthy (n = 229), diagnosed with IBD (n = 101), or suffered from other gastrointestinal conditions ('non-IBD', n = 78).
source: The final dataset included individuals who were healthy (n = 229), diagnosed with IBD (n = 101), or suffered from other gastrointestinal conditions ('non-IBD', n = 78).
evidence: This describes the sample group composition.

claim: The estimated number of populations based on the occurrence of bacterial single-copy core genes (SCGs) present in these metagenomes was higher in healthy individuals than those diagnosed with IBD.
source: In accordance with previous observations of reduced microbial diversity in IBD (Kostic et al., 2014; Nagalingam and Lynch, 2012; Knox et al., 2019), the estimated number of populations based on the occurrence of bacterial single-copy core genes (SCGs) present in these metagenomes was higher in healthy individuals than those diagnosed with IBD (Appendix 1—figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1 and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Without normalizing, module copy numbers were overall higher in healthy samples.
source: Without normalizing, module copy numbers were overall higher in healthy samples (Figure 2A) and modules exhibited weak differential occurrence between cohorts (Figure 2B and C, Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, 2C, and Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Without normalization, modules exhibited weak differential occurrence between cohorts.
source: Without normalizing, module copy numbers were overall higher in healthy samples (Figure 2A) and modules exhibited weak differential occurrence between cohorts (Figure 2B and C, Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The application of PPCN reversed the trend of higher module copy numbers in healthy samples, and most metabolic modules were elevated in IBD.
source: The application of PPCN reversed this trend, and most metabolic modules were elevated in IBD (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: A set of 33 metabolic modules were significantly enriched in metagenomes obtained from individuals diagnosed with IBD.
source: This stringent filtering revealed a set of 33 metabolic modules that were significantly enriched in metagenomes obtained from individuals diagnosed with IBD (Figure 2D and E), 17 of which matched the modules that were associated with HMI previously (Watson et al., 2023; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and 2F, and by statistical analysis described in the methods.

claim: 17 of the 33 IBD-enriched metabolic modules matched the modules that were associated with HMI previously.
source: This stringent filtering revealed a set of 33 metabolic modules that were significantly enriched in metagenomes obtained from individuals diagnosed with IBD (Figure 2D and E), 17 of which matched the modules that were associated with HMI previously (Watson et al., 2023; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with Watson et al., 2023 and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The majority of the metabolic modules that were significantly enriched in the microbiomes of IBD patients encoded biosynthetic capabilities (23 out of 33).
source: The majority of the metabolic modules that were significantly enriched in the microbiomes of IBD patients encoded biosynthetic capabilities (23 out of 33) that resolved to amino acid metabolism (33%), carbohydrate metabolism (21%), cofactor and vitamin biosynthesis (15%), nucleotide biosynthesis (12%), lipid biosynthesis (6%), and energy metabolism (6%) (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is supported by functional categorization of the 33 enriched modules.

claim: The IBD-enriched biosynthetic modules resolved to amino acid metabolism (33%), carbohydrate metabolism (21%), cofactor and vitamin biosynthesis (15%), nucleotide biosynthesis (12%), lipid biosynthesis (6%), and energy metabolism (6%).
source: The majority of the metabolic modules that were significantly enriched in the microbiomes of IBD patients encoded biosynthetic capabilities (23 out of 33) that resolved to amino acid metabolism (33%), carbohydrate metabolism (21%), cofactor and vitamin biosynthesis (15%), nucleotide biosynthesis (12%), lipid biosynthesis (6%), and energy metabolism (6%) (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is supported by functional categorization of the 33 enriched modules.

claim: Amino acid synthesis and carbohydrate metabolism were not reduced in the IBD gut microbiome in this dataset, in contrast to previous reports based on reference genomes.
source: In contrast to previous reports based on reference genomes (Gevers et al., 2014; Morgan et al., 2012), amino acid synthesis and carbohydrate metabolism were not reduced in the IBD gut microbiome in our dataset.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with previous literature.

claim: The results were in accordance with a more recent finding that predicted amino acid secretion potential is increased in the microbiomes of individuals with IBD.
source: Rather, our results were in accordance with a more recent finding that predicted amino acid secretion potential is increased in the microbiomes of individuals with IBD (Heinken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinken et al., 2021.

claim: Within the set of 33 IBD-enriched modules, all the biosynthesis and central carbohydrate modules are directly or indirectly linked via shared enzymes and metabolites.
source: Within our set of 33 modules that were enriched in IBD, it is notable that all the biosynthesis and central carbohydrate modules are directly or indirectly linked via shared enzymes and metabolites.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the metabolic network properties of the enriched modules.

claim: Each enriched module shared on average 25.6% of its enzymes and 40.2% of metabolites with the other enriched modules.
source: Each enriched module shared on average 25.6% of its enzymes and 40.2% of metabolites with the other enriched modules, and overall 18.2% of enzymes and 20.4% of compounds across these modules were shared (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of shared components among the enriched modules.

claim: Overall 18.2% of enzymes and 20.4% of compounds across the enriched modules were shared.
source: Each enriched module shared on average 25.6% of its enzymes and 40.2% of metabolites with the other enriched modules, and overall 18.2% of enzymes and 20.4% of compounds across these modules were shared (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of shared components among the enriched modules.

claim: The few standalone modules that were enriched included the efflux pump MepA and the beta-lactam resistance system, which are associated with drug resistance.
source: The few standalone modules that were enriched included the efflux pump MepA and the beta-lactam resistance system, which are associated with drug resistance.
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of specific enriched modules.

claim: Antibiotics are a common treatment for IBDs.
source: These capacities may provide an advantage since antibiotics are a common treatment for IBDs (Nitzan et al., 2016), but are not necessarily related to the systematic enrichment of biosynthesis modules that likely provide resilience to general environmental stress rather than to a specific stressor such as antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nitzan et al., 2016.

claim: All cohorts within a given group exhibited similar distributions of PPCN values, indicating that the trends result from an overall between-group difference in signal rather than a cohort-specific signal.
source: All cohorts within a given group exhibited similar distributions of PPCN values, which indicates that the trends we observed above result from an overall between-group difference in signal rather than a cohort-specific signal (Appendix 1—figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by per-cohort analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 6B and C.

claim: A smaller proportion of genes resolved to known functions in metagenomic assemblies of samples from healthy individuals compared to the samples from individuals who were diagnosed with IBD.
source: For instance, we noticed that, independent of the annotation strategy, a smaller proportion of genes resolved to known functions in metagenomic assemblies of samples from healthy individuals compared to the samples from individuals who were diagnosed with IBD (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: 84% of KEGG modules (98 out of 118) have significantly lower median copy numbers in the healthy group.
source: Indeed, we found that the normalized copy numbers of most metabolic modules were reduced in the healthy group, where 84% of KEGG modules (98 out of 118) have significantly lower median copy numbers (Appendix 1—figure 5C, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5C.

claim: HMI reference genomes were present in a significantly higher proportion of IBD samples compared to non-HMI genomes.
source: Our read recruitment analysis showed that HMI reference genomes were present in a significantly higher proportion of IBD samples compared to non-HMI genomes (Figure 3B, p < 1e-5, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by read recruitment analysis and statistical testing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fraction of HMI populations was significantly higher within a given IBD sample compared to samples classified as 'non-IBD' and those from healthy individuals.
source: Similarly, the fraction of HMI populations was significantly higher within a given IBD sample compared to samples classified as 'non-IBD' and those from healthy individuals (Figure 3C, p < 1e-24, Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The detection of HMI populations and non-HMI populations was similar in healthy individuals.
source: In contrast, the detection of HMI populations and non-HMI populations was similar in healthy individuals (Figure 3B, p = 0.267, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The intestinal environment of healthy individuals likely supports both HMI and non-HMI populations, wherein 'metabolic diversity' is maintained by metabolic interactions such as cross-feeding.
source: The intestinal environment of healthy individuals likely supports both HMI and non-HMI populations, wherein 'metabolic diversity' is maintained by metabolic interactions such as cross-feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that both HMI and non-HMI populations are detected similarly in healthy individuals.

claim: Loss of cross-feeding interactions in the gut microbiome appears to be associated with a number of human diseases, including IBD.
source: Indeed, loss of cross-feeding interactions in the gut microbiome appears to be associated with a number of human diseases, including IBD (Marcelino et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marcelino et al., 2023.

claim: The top two HMI-associated modules are required for the synthesis of cobalamin from glutamate.
source: This interpretation is further supported by the fact that the top two HMI-associated modules are required for the synthesis of cobalamin from glutamate.
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the top HMI-associated modules.

claim: Auxotrophy for cobalamin biosynthesis is common among gut bacteria that rely on cross-feeding for this essential cofactor.
source: Auxotrophy for cobalamin biosynthesis is common among gut bacteria that rely on cross-feeding for this essential cofactor (Degnan et al., 2014a; Magnúsdóttir et al., 2015; Kelly et al., 2019) (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degnan et al., 2014a; Magnúsdóttir et al., 2015; Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: The classifier correctly identified (on average) 76.8% of samples from individuals diagnosed with IBD and 89.5% of samples representing healthy individuals.
source: It correctly identified (on average) 76.8% of samples from individuals diagnosed with IBD and 89.5% of samples representing healthy individuals, for an overall accuracy of 85.6% and an average AUROCC of 0.832 (Supplementary file 4c).
evidence: This is based on cross-validation analysis of the classifier.

claim: The classifier had an overall accuracy of 85.6% and an average AUROCC of 0.832.
source: It correctly identified (on average) 76.8% of samples from individuals diagnosed with IBD and 89.5% of samples representing healthy individuals, for an overall accuracy of 85.6% and an average AUROCC of 0.832 (Supplementary file 4c).
evidence: This is based on cross-validation analysis of the classifier.

claim: The model outperforms previous attempts to classify IBD from fecal samples in more restrictively defined cohorts.
source: Our model outperforms (Gevers et al., 2014; Halfvarson et al., 2017; Reiter et al., 2022) or has comparable performance to Franzosa et al., 2019; Papa et al., 2012 the previous attempts to classify IBD from fecal samples in more restrictively defined cohorts.
evidence: This is based on comparison with performance metrics from previous studies.

claim: The model has comparable performance to Franzosa et al., 2019 and Papa et al., 2012.
source: Our model outperforms (Gevers et al., 2014; Halfvarson et al., 2017; Reiter et al., 2022) or has comparable performance to Franzosa et al., 2019; Papa et al., 2012 the previous attempts to classify IBD from fecal samples in more restrictively defined cohorts.
evidence: This is based on comparison with performance metrics from previous studies.

claim: The model has the advantage of being a simple model, utilizing a relatively low number of features compared to the other classifiers.
source: It also has the advantage of being a simple model, utilizing a relatively low number of features compared to the other classifiers.
evidence: This is based on comparison of model complexity with previous approaches.

claim: The gradient of metabolic independence reflected by per-population module copy number and the relative increase in the number of HMI populations detected in non-IBD samples suggests that the degree of HMI in the gut microbiome may be indicative of general gut stress.
source: Yet, the gradient of metabolic independence reflected by per-population module copy number and the relative increase in the number of HMI populations detected in non-IBD samples (Appendix 1—figure 5B, Figure 3C) suggests that the degree of HMI in the gut microbiome may be indicative of general gut stress, such as the stress induced by antibiotic use.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5B and Figure 3C.

claim: Antibiotics can cause long-lasting perturbations of the gut microbiome – including reduced diversity, emergence of opportunistic pathogens, increased microbial load, and development of highly resistant strains – with potential implications for host health.
source: Antibiotics can cause long-lasting perturbations of the gut microbiome – including reduced diversity, emergence of opportunistic pathogens, increased microbial load, and development of highly resistant strains – with potential implications for host health (Ramirez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2020.

claim: The resulting pattern of sample classification corresponds to the posttreatment decline and subsequent recovery of species richness documented in the study by Palleja et al., 2018.
source: The resulting pattern of sample classification corresponds to the posttreatment decline and subsequent recovery of species richness documented in the study by Palleja et al., 2018.
evidence: This is based on application of the classifier to the Palleja et al., 2018 dataset and comparison with their findings.

claim: All pretreatment samples were classified as 'healthy' followed by a decline in the proportion of 'healthy' samples to a minimum 8 days posttreatment, and a gradual increase until 180 days posttreatment, when over 90% of samples were classified as 'healthy'.
source: All pretreatment samples were classified as 'healthy' followed by a decline in the proportion of 'healthy' samples to a minimum 8 days posttreatment, and a gradual increase until 180 days posttreatment, when over 90% of samples were classified as 'healthy' (Figure 5, Supplementary file 4b).
evidence: This is based on classifier predictions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The increase in the HMI metric serves as an indicator of stress in the gut microbiome, regardless of whether that stress arises from the IBD condition or the application of antibiotics.
source: In other words, the increase in the HMI metric serves as an indicator of stress in the gut microbiome, regardless of whether that stress arises from the IBD condition or the application of antibiotics.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the classifier's performance across different stress conditions.

claim: Environmental stress in the human gut – whether it is associated with inflammation, cancer, or antibiotic use – promotes the survival and relative expansion of microbial populations with HMI.
source: Overall, our observations that stem from the analysis of hundreds of reference genomes, deeply sequenced gut metagenomes, and multiple categories of human disease states suggest that environmental stress in the human gut – whether it is associated with inflammation, cancer, or antibiotic use – promotes the survival and relative expansion of microbial populations with HMI.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from multiple analyses in the study.

claim: HMI is a high-level metric to classify gradients of human health states through the gut microbiota that is robust to ethnic, geographical, or lifestyle factors.
source: These results establish HMI as a high-level metric to classify gradients of human health states through the gut microbiota that is robust to ethnic, geographical, or lifestyle factors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the classifier's performance across diverse cohorts.

claim: The reduction in microbial diversity, or more generally 'dysbiosis', is an emergent property of microbial communities responding to disease pathogenesis or other external factors such as antibiotic use that disrupt the gut microbial ecosystem.
source: Taken together with recent evidence that models altered ecological relationships within gut microbiomes under stress due to disrupted metabolic cross-feeding (Heinken et al., 2021; Marcelino et al., 2023), our data support the hypothesis that the reduction in microbial diversity, or more generally 'dysbiosis', is an emergent property of microbial communities responding to disease pathogenesis or other external factors such as antibiotic use that disrupt the gut microbial ecosystem.
evidence: This is an interpretation that integrates the current findings with previous literature.

claim: This paradigm depicts microbes as bystanders by default, rather than perpetrators or drivers of noncommunicable human diseases.
source: This paradigm depicts microbes as bystanders by default, rather than perpetrators or drivers of noncommunicable human diseases, and provides an ecological framework to explain the frequently observed reduction in microbial diversity associated with IBD and other noncommunicable human diseases and disorders.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ecological implications of the findings.

claim: The paradigm provides an ecological framework to explain the frequently observed reduction in microbial diversity associated with IBD and other noncommunicable human diseases and disorders.
source: This paradigm depicts microbes as bystanders by default, rather than perpetrators or drivers of noncommunicable human diseases, and provides an ecological framework to explain the frequently observed reduction in microbial diversity associated with IBD and other noncommunicable human diseases and disorders.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ecological implications of the findings.

claim: The PPCN estimates the proportion of microbes in a community with a particular metabolic capacity by normalizing observed metabolic module copy numbers with the 'number of microbial populations in a given metagenome'.
source: Briefly, the PPCN estimates the proportion of microbes in a community with a particular metabolic capacity (Figure 1, Appendix 1—figure 2) by normalizing observed metabolic module copy numbers with the 'number of microbial populations in a given metagenome', which we estimate using the SCGs without relying on the reconstruction of individual genomes.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for PPCN calculation, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Validation of the PPCN method using simulated metagenomic data demonstrated that it is accurate in capturing metagenome-level metabolic capacity relative to genome-level metabolic capacity estimated from the same data.
source: Our validation of this method using simulated metagenomic data demonstrated that it is accurate in capturing metagenome-level metabolic capacity relative to genome-level metabolic capacity estimated from the same data (Appendix 2, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on validation analysis described in Appendix 2.

claim: Of the final set of 338 reference genomes that passed filters, 258 (76.3%) resolved to Firmicutes, 60 (17.8%) to Bacteroidetes, and 20 (5.9%) to Proteobacteria.
source: Of the final set of 338 reference genomes that passed our filters, 258 (76.3%) resolved to Firmicutes, 60 (17.8%) to Bacteroidetes, and 20 (5.9%) to Proteobacteria.
evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the reference genome set.

claim: Most of the reference genomes resolved to families common to the colonic microbiota, such as Lachnospiraceae (30.0%), Ruminococcaceae/Oscillospiraceae (23.1%), and Bacteroidaceae (10.1%).
source: Most of these genomes resolved to families common to the colonic microbiota, such as Lachnospiraceae (30.0%), Ruminococcaceae/Oscillospiraceae (23.1%), and Bacteroidaceae (10.1%) (Arumugam et al., 2011), while 5.9% belonged to poorly studied families with temporary code names (Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the reference genome set, with citation to Arumugam et al., 2011.

claim: A given genome was assumed to have HMI if its average completeness of the 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules was at least 80%, equivalent to a summed metabolic independence score of 26.4.
source: We assumed that a given genome had HMI if its average completeness of the 33 HMI-associated metabolic modules was at least 80%, equivalent to a summed metabolic independence score of 26.4 (Methods).
evidence: This describes the threshold used to classify genomes as HMI.

claim: Several species in the Bacteroides group were not classified as HMI despite their frequent dominance of the gut microbiome of individuals with IBD.
source: Given the number of ways a genome can pass or fail this threshold, this arbitrary cutoff has significant shortcomings, which was demonstrated by the fact that several species in the Bacteroides group were not classified as HMI despite their frequent dominance of the gut microbiome of individuals with IBD (Saitoh et al., 2002; Wexler, 2007; Vineis et al., 2016) (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a limitation of the HMI classification approach, supported by citations to Saitoh et al., 2002; Wexler, 2007; Vineis et al., 2016.

claim: The genomes that were classified as HMI by this approach were consistently higher in their detection and abundance in IBD samples.
source: That said, the genomes that were classified as HMI by this approach were consistently higher in their detection and abundance in IBD samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Across all genomes, the mean metabolic independence score was 24.0 (Q1: 19.9, Q3: 25.7).
source: Across all genomes, the mean metabolic independence score was 24.0 (Q1: 19.9, Q3: 25.7).
evidence: This is a summary statistic of the metabolic independence scores.

claim: 17.5% (59) of the reference genomes were identified as HMI.
source: We identified 17.5% (59) of the reference genomes as HMI.
evidence: This describes the proportion of genomes classified as HMI.

claim: HMI genomes were on average substantially larger (3.8 Mbp) than non-HMI genomes (2.9 Mbp).
source: HMI genomes were on average substantially larger (3.8 Mbp) than non-HMI genomes (2.9 Mbp) and encoded more genes (3634 vs 2683 genes, respectively), which is in accordance with the reduced metabolic potential of non-HMI populations (Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of genome sizes between HMI and non-HMI genomes.

claim: HMI genomes encoded more genes (3634) than non-HMI genomes (2683 genes).
source: HMI genomes were on average substantially larger (3.8 Mbp) than non-HMI genomes (2.9 Mbp) and encoded more genes (3634 vs 2683 genes, respectively), which is in accordance with the reduced metabolic potential of non-HMI populations (Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene counts between HMI and non-HMI genomes.

claim: Survival in a disturbed gut environment will likely require a wide variety of additional functions that are not covered in the list of metabolic modules considered to determine HMI status.
source: We note that survival in a disturbed gut environment will likely require a wide variety of additional functions that are not covered in the list of metabolic modules we consider to determine HMI status – e.g., see Degnan et al., 2014b; Martens et al., 2014; Zong et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020; Goodman et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2016.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There may be many ways for a microbe to be metabolically independent, and the strategy used likely failed to identify some HMI populations.
source: Indeed, there may be many ways for a microbe to be metabolically independent, and our strategy likely failed to identify some HMI populations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations of the HMI classification approach.

claim: For those studies reporting accuracy, a maximum accuracy of 77% was achieved based on either metabolite profiles (for prediction of IBD subtype) or k-mer-based sequence variants (for differentiating between IBD and non-IBD samples).
source: For those studies reporting accuracy, a maximum accuracy of 77% was achieved based on either metabolite profiles (for prediction of IBD subtype) (Franzosa et al., 2019) or k-mer-based sequence variants (for differentiating between IBD and non-IBD samples) (Reiter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on review of previous classifier studies.

claim: For AUROCC metric, the highest value was 0.92, achieved by Franzosa et al., 2019, when using metabolite profiles, with or without species abundance data, for classifying IBD vs non-IBD.
source: For this metric the highest value was 0.92, achieved by Franzosa et al., 2019, when using metabolite profiles, with or without species abundance data, for classifying IBD vs non-IBD.
evidence: This is based on review of previous classifier studies.

claim: The majority of previous classifiers were trained and tested on a relatively small group of individuals that all come from the same region.
source: However, the majority of these classifiers were trained and tested on a relatively small group of individuals that all come from the same region, i.e., clinical studies confined to a specific hospital.
evidence: This is based on review of previous classifier studies.

claim: Previous classifiers either relied on data that are inaccessible to most laboratories and clinics or they required complex k-mer-based models without the resolution to differentiate gradients in host health.
source: Though some had high performance, they either relied on data that are inaccessible to most laboratories and clinics considering that untargeted metabolomics analyses are difficult to reproduce (Koek et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020), or they required complex k-mer-based models without the resolution to differentiate gradients in host health (Reiter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on review and critique of previous classifier approaches, with citations to Koek et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020; Reiter et al., 2022.

claim: Most identified modules (89.4%; 95% CI: [87.5%, 91.3%]) on the training sets remain significant at a slightly less stringent threshold (1e-8) on the validation sets in repeated sample-split analysis.
source: We repeat this sample split analysis 1000 times with an FDR-adjusted p-value threshold of 1e-10 on the first split; most identified modules (89.4%; 95% CI: [87.5%, 91.3%]) on the training sets remain significant at a slightly less stringent threshold (1e-8) on the validation sets.
evidence: This is based on repeated sample-split validation analysis.

claim: The approach used to identify IBD-enriched modules yields stable and statistically significant results on this dataset.
source: This indicates that the approach we used to identify IBD-enriched modules yields stable and statistically significant results on this dataset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the validation analysis results.
